prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, enabling optical frequency standards at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is the one shortlisted candidate where a simple, surprising idea (a magic wavelength at which the lattice light shifts the upper and lower clock levels equally, so the atoms can be held tightly without disturbing the transition) was turned into a measurement that revealed new physics-ready territory. Katori proposed the idea and made the first strontium lattice clock; Ye's group then showed what many atoms probed together can do, reaching fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, resolving gravitational redshift over millimetres, and exposing many-body and spin-exchange effects in the clock. The result has been reproduced and surpassed in several independent laboratories (Sr, Yb, Hg), with routine international comparisons, so the interpretation is stable and not resting on one measurement. It makes a quantitative statement about how time runs inside a sample and where relativity and quantum mechanics meet, which is the kind of fundamental question I care about, and it also has the typical long tail of unforeseen use (geodesy, dark-matter and constant-variation searches, a redefinition of the second). Two names give a clean allocation. Having done systematic-shift and atomic-structure calculations of this kind, I can judge that the uncertainty budgets are credible.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty and overlap: the frequency comb (2005) and ion control (2012) already honour the technical foundations of optical clocks, and one can argue the lattice clock is a refinement of a rewarded line. It is also instrument-heavy and its signature societal outcome, the redefinition of the SI second, has not yet happened. Finally, other realisations (Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow, Sterr, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) and ion-clock groups have real claims, so the line around the invention is a judgement. I also have to admit that I am a close reader of this field, which could bias me toward valuing it.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B008 first because the lattice clock opens new observational regimes (relativistic geodesy, constants, dark-matter searches, redefinition of the second) with a clean Katori-Ye pair, while noting the Hall/Hansch and Wineland overlap and competing realisations.
responses.response: I agree with the pair and the maturity argument. On the overlap worry I would be firmer than he is: the comb is a readout tool and the Wineland work is about single trapped ions, whereas the lattice clock's distinct contribution is the magic-wavelength trapping of very many neutral atoms, which is what changes the statistical limit and allows the 1e-18 regime and the many-body effects. I would draft the citation around that invention so the earlier prizes are visibly not repeated. I disagree only mildly on the redefinition of the second: I do not think we need to wait for it, since the scientific case stands on the comparisons already done.

responses.point: Johansson places circuit QED first as a clean new regime (microwave quantum optics on a chip) behind essentially all superconducting qubits, but flags overlap with the 2025 circuits prize, credit for Girvin and Huard, and his own proximity to the community.
responses.response: I take the scientific case seriously and I do not equate my first place with a lower merit for B012. My difficulty is the combination of three things: the 2025 prize was just given for superconducting circuits, the credited trio omits Girvin and Yale co-authors who wrote the 2004 proposal, and the strongest recent impact is technological (qubit architecture) rather than a new finding about nature. I would not put B012 in the preferred configuration, but I accept it as a serious future candidate. I also appreciate that he flagged his own possible conflict; I have flagged mine below.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Higgs observation by ATLAS and CMS first as the clearest experimental clue in fundamental physics, the natural experimental complement to the 2013 theory prize, with the unresolved problem of fitting two collaborations of thousands into three people.
responses.response: I agree on the importance and the maturity, and I defer to him and others on particle physics. Where I qualify his view is that the scientific merit is not in dispute, the attribution is. Choosing three of four named founders (he drops Jenni, others drop Virdee or Della Negra) is by his own admission a judgement call, and a prize built on that cannot be defended on the record alone. That is why I rank it as an alternative rather than my choice, not because it is smaller science. If the committee finds an attribution formula it trusts, I would not object to B056.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect first as a new state of matter, a clean theory-experiment story (Kane-Mele, Molenkamp), independently confirmed over two decades.
responses.response: I find the idea convincing and the confirmation robust, and I would be comfortable with B049 as the condensed-matter alternative. My reservation, shared in different words by Johansson and by his own list of uncertainties, is the missing Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that directly led to Molenkamp's HgTe experiment, together with the separate 3D topological insulator story. If the committee can settle that credit, I would support it; for now the attribution gap is larger than for the lattice clock.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues judge the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
How much weight to give the still-pending redefinition of the SI second, and whether Katori-Ye is a fair boundary against other lattice-clock groups and ion-clock work.

For the Higgs and topological insulator alternatives, whether a defensible attribution formula exists (three of four ATLAS/CMS leaders; the missing HgTe theory proposers); I defer to colleagues in particle and condensed-matter physics.
statement.conflict_note: I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have worked with the Lund and Keller attosecond groups, which is relevant to atomic, molecular and optical physics candidates generally and could be seen as a proximity issue. No specific personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye or their groups is apparent from my profile, so I do not see a recusal requirement for B008, but I note my field proximity.
